Ineffable

in-EF-uh-bul · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ineffable is too great, intense, or sacred to be expressed or described in words.

The grandmother's expression as she held her first great-grandchild for the very first time carried an ineffable joy that none of the family's photographs quite managed to preserve.

Worked Example

Musicians often say that the exact feeling a piece of music gives them is ineffable -- something they can play or hear, but never fully explain in plain sentences.

Ineffable names an experience or feeling so intense or profound that ordinary language simply falls short of describing it.

How Ineffable Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

indescribable

indescribable: too great or unusual to be described

unutterable

unutterable: too intense to be spoken or expressed

Antonyms

describable

describable: able to be put into words

mundane

mundane: ordinary, lacking anything remarkable

How Strong Is It? — remarkable → ineffable → transcendent

remarkable vs. ineffable

remarkable vs. ineffable: Remarkable just means noteworthy or impressive -- it can still be described perfectly well in ordinary sentences.

transcendent vs. ineffable

transcendent vs. ineffable: Transcendent goes even further than ineffable, suggesting an experience that reaches beyond ordinary human experience entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root (not standalone) — effable

root (not standalone) — effable: able to be spoken out loud -- not a standalone English word on its own, from Latin ex-/ef- ('out') + fari ('to speak') (Latin effabilis)

Put it together

Put it together: Ineffable comes from Latin in- ('not') + effabilis ('able to be spoken'), itself from ex-/ef- ('out') + fari ('to speak'). There's no separate English word 'effable' to peel off cleanly -- but that same fari root, 'to speak,' also hides inside this unit's own affable (literally 'easy to speak to'). Two words in one lesson, one shared ancient root.

Use the root in a new word: affable

Use the root in a new word: affable: You'll meet affable later in this very unit -- it shares ineffable's Latin root fari, 'to speak.'

Word Choice

Ineffable is a formal, almost reverent word -- reach for it when a feeling or experience is so intense that ordinary words genuinely fail, not for everyday mild surprise.
